**Commentary of al-Biqa'i (*Nazm al-Durar*) on Surah 90 (al-Balad), verse 1:**

[p. 45] **Surat al-Balad: its purpose**

It is to show that power is denied to man and affirmed for his Creator, the Lord of Judgment, through mention of the one among them who is saved, who leads to happiness in the Hereafter, and this is what his Lord, glorified is He, guided him to. That is the meaning of its name. For whoever reflects on the security of the people of the Sacred Precinct (*ahl al-Haram*), and on the provision and goodness they enjoy despite the scarcity of provision in their land, while others who are more numerous and stronger than they are subject to fear and hunger, will know that this is by ﴿the name of God﴾, the sole King, the Subduer, ﴿the Compassionate﴾, who bestowed His blessing upon all His creatures and varied His gifts among them, so that each one is discontented with his condition, in toil over what concerns him in his private and public affairs, by a wisdom that thought cannot grasp; ﴿the Merciful﴾, who singled out the people of His friendship with what pleases Him of His decrees, so He brings them to His Garden and saves them from the Fire.

* *

When He concluded the words of Surat al-Fajr with the Garden, which is the best of the places in which creatures dwell, especially the one attributed to His most particular name, which indicates that it is the best of gardens, [p. 46] and after He concluded its verses with the soul at peace, following mention of the commanding self that falls into the depths of regret, for which one wishes non-existence, and after what preceded [indicating] that it is still in the struggle of life's trials in ease and hardship, He opened this surah with the commanding self, swearing an oath concerning its matter by the greatest of lands and the most noble of the possessors of the soul at peace. He said, emphasizing with the negative, since it negates the opposite of what is established in the content of the speech, while being certain that He did not intend anything other than that: ﴿I do not swear﴾, meaning, I swear an oath whose content I affirm and whose opposite I negate. It is possible that the negation is to be taken at face value, and the meaning is that the matter is evident and needs no oath, even by this oath which you know to be of the utmost greatness. This is like His saying, ﴿So I swear by the positions of the stars﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:75] ﴿And indeed, it is a mighty oath, if you only knew﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:76]. ﴿By this city﴾, meaning the Sacred one, which is Makkah, which those who seek it do not reach except with great exertion, and yet they only increase in their love for it. This indicates that God, the Exalted, made it the best of lands, and cast its love into the hearts of those whom He chose from every settler and nomad, because it was honored at its beginning, its end, and its middle by the best of servants. He did not describe it as secure, because that does not suit the context of hardship, unlike what is in al-Tin, where the intended meaning there is perfections.

When the land was magnified by God's oath by it, He increased it in greatness by the state of the Prophet within it, indicating that the honour of the place is by the honour of its inhabitants. This comes in a circumstantial clause, so He said: ﴿And you﴾, meaning, you are the best of everyone who is present or who dwells in the desert, ﴿are a resident﴾, that is, one who dwells, or ﴿lawful﴾ for you, what is not lawful for others, namely killing whomever you wish of those who claim that no one has power over them, ﴿in this land﴾. So you may make lawful the killing of Ibn Khatal and others, even if he is clinging to the curtains of the Ka'bah, and you may make unlawful the killing of whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan, and other things that God did for you after the Hijrah, a long time after the revelation of this Meccan surah, as a sign among the signs of prophethood. Or, in meaning: its people make lawful against you, although you are the most noble of creation, what they do not make lawful against game or trees. He repeated the explicit mention of the land and did not use a pronoun, to increase its glorification and to denounce what they consider lawful of harming the believers within it, and as an indication that He takes pleasure in mentioning it.

Thus the oath has been sworn by the lord of lands and the lord of servants. Every kind has a lord, which is its highest point of nobility. The noblest of inanimate things is the ruby, and it is its lord. Were it to rise above this nobility, it would become a plant that grows, as in Paradise. The noblest kind of plant is the palm tree, and were it to rise above that, it would become an animal that moves by will. So the animal is the lord of created beings, and its lord is the human being, because of the speech and eloquence he possesses. The lord of humans is the messengers, may the best of prayers and peace be upon them, because of their great connection with the King, the Judge. Their lord is the noblest of creation (ﷺ), with whom they were sealed, because of the virtues in which he excelled, the highest of which is this Qur'an. So the lord of creation, Muhammad son of Abdullah, the Messenger of God, is the noblest of possible beings and their lord, because he reached the highest station that can be attained by them. Had there remained above that any station that a possible being could attain, he would have been transferred to it. And because he was the most noble, his trials were the greatest of trials. He bore the harm of his people through words that are more piercing than arrows. They placed the entrails of a camel on his noble back, (we would ransom him with the free faces and protected foreheads and cheeks of ourselves), while he was prostrating. They placed thorns in his path, and there was a consensus against him, aiming at him with every kind of harm, including imprisonment, exile, and killing, to the extent that he (ﷺ) said:

"No one has been harmed for the sake of God as I have been harmed."

(p-49) Since this condition made clear that the oath is in reality by him (ﷺ), He repeated the oath by him in a way that includes others, saying: ﴿and by the begetter﴾. Since the purpose is to draw wonder at the origin of creation through procreation, from every living thing, in all matters of procreation, and at what man has of speech, expression, and marvelous understanding, and since the context is a rebuke of the people of the commanding self (al-nafs al-ammarah), who are the majority of mankind, the expression with the particle used for non-rational things was fitting, because it is one of the particles of wonder. So He said: ﴿and what he begot﴾, that is, whether male or female, whoever it may be. Thus the Prophet (ﷺ) entered, as already mentioned, and became one by whom He swears repeatedly. Likewise his parents, Ibrahim and his son Isma'il, (p-49) peace be upon them both, entered, along with what they did and what Allah did for them in that land. It is known that mentioning the work is an indication of its maker. The intended meaning is therefore an oath by Him who made the land what it is in its majesty, who singled out the Prophet (ﷺ) with the mission He bestowed upon him, and who differentiated among those who beget and are begotten in their qualities, in deficiency and perfection and all other conditions, as an indication of the perfection He possesses in majesty and beauty. Perhaps He singled out these things for the oath as consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) and as strengthening him to bear harm, indicating that whoever has been decreed to remain in hardship should choose that this hardship be in what pleases Allah, glory be to Him and exalted. This is because the Prophet (ﷺ) was in Makkah the Honored, in the greatest severity of what he suffered from the harm of the disbelievers, both to himself and to his companions, may Allah be pleased with them, because of the elevation of his station, for the severity of trial falls upon the most excellent, then the next most excellent, as already mentioned, along with his command (ﷺ) to patience and forgiveness. Every parent and every child is in hardship through parenthood and childhood, and other countless human distresses, from the time he is a drop of semen in three darknesses, in the narrowness of a passage and a dwelling place, then birth, then being bound in a cradle, then weaning away from familiarity and family; (p-50) from the disciplinarian and the teacher, the rebuke of the elders, the opposition of peers, and whoever among women dominates over him; along with his being prone to illnesses and all other things he dislikes of ailments and aims, poverty, calamities and afflictions, demands and needs. He does not attain his desire, does not reach his aim, does not obtain what he chooses, and in most cases does not escape what he fears. The details of this summary cannot be counted, and they have no limit to be exhausted, extending to death and what follows it. Therefore the thing sworn about is His saying:

﴿We have indeed created﴾, that is, with the complete power and the incomparable majesty that We possess, ﴿man﴿, that is, this species, ﴿in toil﴾, that is, in severe hardship and great difficulty, surrounding him as a container surrounds what it holds. Had He, glory be to Him and exalted, left him to himself in any part of it, he would have perished. Were it not for these trials, he would have claimed for himself what is not fitting for him of great attributes. Some of them nonetheless claimed divinity, and some claimed union (ittihad) with the Lord of the servants. Exalted is Allah above their manifestly corrupt saying, for what He, glory be to Him and exalted, joined to him of death, sickness and all other afflictions. He, glory be to Him, did this so that the weakness and incapacity of the servant would become manifest, along with what He granted him of outward and inward faculties in speech, action, seizing and intellect, and so that the perfection of His knowledge and the comprehensiveness of His power would be shown. And so that whoever is created upon this attribute would become manifest to Him. He knew all that is in the surah, so He knew with certainty the denial of his assumption (p-51) of the limitlessness of His power and the sublimity of His greatness, and the corruption of this assumption by the witness of reason, from the standpoint that he is a created thing, and by the witness of existence, because he follows the path of evil and cannot reach the path of good except through divine success. He knew with certainty the inimitability of the surah, because no creature has the power to produce a single sentence that gathers all the sentences that follow it. This is in addition to the varieties of concision it contains, which reach the limit of inimitability, and in addition to the inimitability of the rest of its sentences in the beauty of their arrangement, the firmness of their composition, their interconnection, and the attention paid to matching words with meanings, and other matters whose full extent cannot be reached by any but Him, glory be to Him and exalted is His station. He also knew that honour and humiliation do not revolve around worldly ease and constriction, as its explanation has already passed in the commentary on Surat al-Fajr. And because He knew that man is always in distress, hardship and fatigue, first from his need for mere movement and rest, second for food and drink, and third for what follows from these two, and other things whose enumeration is wearying and whose limits are unknown, the denial in His saying, exalted be He, was directed at explaining the causes that bring him into distress. These are two desires: a psychic desire and a sensory desire. The psychic desire is restricted to four. The first is that he desires that everyone in existence be in his grip, so He pointed to it with ...

(p. 52) That is, this human being, because of the weakness of his intellect and despite what he is in of various kinds of hardships, ﴿thinks that no one⁠﴾ — ﴿will have power over him⁠﴾. Since [the verse] emphasized [the negation] with the verbal form and with the specificity of this negative, it placed the prepositional phrase first, as emphasis conveying the concern for the human being. So [God] said: ﴿over him⁠﴾, meaning specifically, ﴿anyone⁠﴾, meaning from among the people of the earth or of the heavens, who would overpower him. Yet he rebels against his Creator even though he sees His power over the like of him, by Himself and by whomever He wills of His hosts. So he opposes His messengers, peace be upon them, and denies His signs.

Imam Abu Ja'far Ibn al-Zubayr said: When the Exalted and Glorified made clear the condition of those whose mention preceded in the two surahs, in their great bewilderment and the evil of their heedlessness, and what that brought upon them of remembrance accompanied by regret, when repentance no longer benefits, and "there is no longer any time for hope" (wa-lāta ḥīna maṭma', an idiom meaning that the moment for hope has passed), He followed that by informing our Prophet, upon whom be the best of prayers and peace, that the occurrence of this from them had proceeded according to the ruling of the precedent (al-sābiqa, the divine preordainment) which He willed, and the wisdom (al-ḥikma) which He had decreed, as came in another place: ﴿Had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance⁠﴾ [al-Sajda: 13]. So the Exalted indicated this by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We created man in toil⁠﴾ [al-Balad: 4], meaning: We created him for this, as a trial, so that this would be a decisive matter for whoever had already been predestined to wretchedness, [preventing him] from reflection and taking heed. ﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will never be guided, ever⁠﴾ [al-Kahf: 57]. So He blinded them by that (p. 53) toil in which He created them, and made their hearts heedless, so they thought that no one had power over them. The Exalted and Glorified has explained this act of His towards them in His saying to His Prophet ﷺ: ﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance and who follows his desire⁠﴾ [al-Kahf: 28], and ﴿Had your Lord willed, all those upon the earth would have believed, all of them⁠﴾ [Yunus: 99]. So you see them, O Muhammad, possessing sight and faculties by which observers take heed: ﴿Did We not make for him two eyes?⁠﴾ [al-Balad: 8] ﴿And a tongue and two lips?⁠﴾ [al-Balad: 9]. Why then did he not undertake the freeing of his own soul, and take heed from his present and his past?

﴿But he has not attempted the ascent⁠﴾ [al-Balad: 11]. However, when God wills evil upon a people, there is no turning it back. — End.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 90, verse 6:

Since a person takes pride in spending only when it leads to poverty, he (the Almighty) knew that the purpose of the allusion is that he has many times what he spent, insofar as He belittled it by the word "destruction" (ihlak), alluding to the second and third of his carnal desires. These are his wish that he be the one to have boasting and obligation over all existing things, and his wish that he have such wealth that thoughts cannot encompass it and the regions cannot contain it, as the hadith indicates: "If the son of Adam had a valley of gold..." and "Nothing fills the belly of the son of Adam except dust." (Glorified and Exalted is He) explained his ignorance in his reckoning of that (p-54) and what followed it with His saying: ﴿He says﴾, that is, boasting of his power and strength: ﴿"I have squandered wealth in abundance."﴾ For the sake of emphasizing its abundance, the reading of [Abu] Ja'far with the doubled letter came, on the basis that it is a plural like rukka'  and raki' (bowing ones), so it conveyed that it is in such a quantity that it cannot be counted; rather, even if it were gathered, the earth would not hold it except by [some of it] being piled upon other parts, so it cannot be counted or limited. That is, this is a small part of the great amount that is with me, with which I have put the bonds of favors around the necks of men, and with which I have enslaved free people in every age; so I have reached the state where, when I call, many answer, when I cry out, many respond, and when I command, many obey, in return for my past favors and in desire for my lasting blessings. So who would disobey me, or who would oppose my command, let alone wish to obscure my remembrance or diminish my standing?

Since a thing is not of concern unless it is unknown, at least in some respects, He denied this supposition on the assumption that it had occurred, for he could not reach what he supposes except by it. This is stated in His words, pointing to his fourth innate desire, which is that his affairs be hidden so that no one at all sees his error: ﴿Does he think﴾ that this stubborn human being, through the smallness of his intellect, ﴿that no one has seen him﴾ with the eye or with insight in the past time, ﴿anyone?﴾ (p-55) That is, in this deed of his, whether secret or open, and in all his affairs, so that he diminishes everything he has done whenever he wishes. And everything of the consequences of these four desires that escapes him, and it always escapes him, causes him, in his striving to attain it, to be in hardship, toil and distress, to the point that he throws himself into ruin to attain it, and never obtains from it what would satisfy him. This is a metaphor for his doing evil deeds as one who thinks that no one is aware of him. Therefore God, exalted is He, warned him with various kinds of warning, so that he might take heed and preserve his life.

When God, glory be to Him and exalted, rebuked him for these shortcomings, He established for him, by means of that which made his sensual desire (al-shahwa al-hissiyya), branching into its kinds, something that necessitates that its Agent, who bestows upon him through some of His overflowing bounty, is knowing of all his affairs, capable of benefiting and harming him by Himself and by whomever of His hosts He wills. So He said, pointing to what follows from the seeing of the eye that perceives and roams the sensible world, and from the looking of the eye of insight that roams the spiritual world, of desire: that he attain, by the eye of his sight, everything he sees, and know by the eye of his insight what is fine (mália), and be freed from everything he sees that is ugly (qabīḥ), and remind him of what he was obligated to give thanks for, by using these faculties in what He has prescribed for him (p-56) and restraining them from what God has forbidden: ﴿Did We not make﴾, that is, by the greatness that We possess, which no one can rival or come near to, ﴿for him two eyes﴾ with which he sees, for otherwise most of what he wishes would be frustrated for him; ﴿We split them﴾ while he was in the womb, in three darknesses, in a proportion suited such that neither of them exceeds the other by anything; and We determined the whiteness and the blackness, or the blueness, or the hazel, or other than that, as you see; and We deposited in them the sight in a manner that creation is unable to comprehend.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 90, verse 9:

When He (glory be to Him) had determined for him that which gives rise to the two desires for attaining what is good and averting what is evil, He followed that with what gives rise to the two desires of commanding and forbidding, and the various perfections of the perfective kind. So He said: ﴿And a tongue﴾, meaning, with which he translates what is in his inner self, ﴿and two lips﴾, meaning, which cover his mouth and assist him in eating and drinking, and in speech with eloquence and rhetorical skill to a known degree that no one else attains, so that his affairs are gathered together and he reaches many aims and momentous matters. He did not mention hearing, because speech implies it. The meaning is: Are We not able, by the power with which We have endowed him to accomplish what has been mentioned, to make for another like what We made for him and more, so that he could contend with him and overcome him?

(p-٥٧) Since God Most High bestows upon every person, at every moment, a fresh favor in preserving these three faculties, He expressed them with the present tense (*mudari'*). Since the blessing of the intellect ('aql, reason) lies in His granting it first and then in guiding its bearer to good second, and since its matter is hidden, and since it is known that no one is guided in all his movements and rests toward what makes him happy, indeed this one who is denied it is not qualified for the path of good, the past tense was chosen for it, to affirm that it is an established existing thing, and to make it an innate disposition (*gharizah*) that does not change and a nature (*tabi'ah*) that does not alter. Rather, it dominates its possessor, leading him to harm or to what he loves and delights in, even if he dislikes it. It is the means by which one is delivered from the evil of those distresses in the abode of happiness. So God Most High said: ﴿And We guided him﴾, that is, by what We gave him of intellect, ﴿to the two highways﴾, that is, the two paths of good and evil. By what We made for him of that, he became hearing, seeing, and knowing, and thus became a locus of moral responsibility (*taklif*).

Al-Tabarani related from Abu Umamah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

"O people! Hasten to your Lord, for that which is little and sufficient is better than that which is abundant and distracting. O people, they are only two highways: the highway of good and the highway of evil. So let not the highway of evil be more beloved to you than the highway of good."

Al-Mundhiri said: *al-najd* here means the path (*tariq*). It is a path in an ascent. He expressed good and evil by it because they elevate a person above the rank of the rest of the animals. And because a person does not choose either of them except with exertion and effort, like the effort of one who climbs a steep ascent. *Al-najd* linguistically means an elevated place. God Most High elevates whomever He wills of them, as He wills, contrary to what the apparent state of a person would require, namely that he does not love to undertake anything at all, and does not want things to come to him except effortlessly. This is for the sake of manifesting His power, glorified and exalted is He.

As for the difficulty of the path of good, it is because it is surrounded by hardships, so that acting upon it becomes the most arduous and difficult of things, although everyone loves its name and meaning. As for the difficulty of the path of evil, it is very evident, although God obliges a person to it when He wills by facilitating it, making it beloved, lightening it and bringing it near, although everyone dislikes its name and recoils from its meaning.

God Most High made the primordial natural disposition (*fitrah*), the sound one upon which He created people, to be upright, such that it perceives evil and forbids it, and perceives good and commands it. Yet the desires and appetites contend with it, and the one who prevails is the one whom God helps. To this point the hadith "If you have no shame, then do what you wish" alludes, and the hadith: "Righteousness is that toward which the soul is at rest (p-٥٩) and the breast is expanded, and sin is that which stirs in the breast and wavers in the heart, even if people give you legal opinions and give you legal opinions."

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 90, verse 11:

Since the meaning of what preceded is that this human being is incapable, however far his strength extends and however high his power reaches, because of the prior saying of Him, exalted is He: ﴿And man was created weak﴾ [An-Nisa: 28], and because all of his affair is known and exposed in his secret just as it is exposed in his open conduct, as indicated by the hadith of Jundub, may Allah be pleased with him, in al-Tabarani: "No servant conceals a secret but Allah clothes him in its garment." And the hadith of Abu Sa'id, may Allah be pleased with him, in Ahmad and Abu Ya'la: "If one of you were to work on a solid rock that has no door and no opening, his work would still come out to the people." So he is reached by it and within its power. And it was obligatory upon him to be grateful for what Allah, glorified and exalted is He, gave him of faculties, which He made instruments for his evil earning, for disbelief. This was caused by His, glorified and exalted is He, saying, detailing the things that lead to comfort in the Hereafter, negating their doing from him in the true sense, as a proof of his incapacity: ﴿But he has not attempted the steep path﴾. That is, he did not leap, and he did not throw himself quickly, forcefully and intensely, to the point that from the intensity of his love for what he sees of good in what he enters, it is as if he came to it without thought or deliberation, but rather rushing headlong, ﴿the steep path﴾, which is the path of salvation. What is established in the language is that it is the path ascending a mountain, and its name has been borrowed for acts of righteousness (p-60) that are established in souls as refreshing and not tiring, while being greater in honour and higher in merit. This is because We have withheld him from it by Our hands, by Our great strength and Our wondrous power. That is because when the good was beloved to hearts, an object of love to souls, desired, from which no one turns away, We made it at the beginning disagreeable [and] difficult and heavy upon souls, until, because it opposes desire, it became as if it were a steep, arduous ascent, which one does not attain the hardship of its climbing except with firm resolve, a passing aspiration, a decisive intention, training and drill, discipline and refinement, intense striving and great struggle against the self, desire and Satan, such that one who undertakes it does so as one throwing himself into it [without] deliberation, like the lover who throws himself in and is consumed by it. So this was the cause that this ignorant man of his own self, who transgresses his bounds, did not choose good for himself with the sight he was given, by which he sees the works of Allah, and the insight by which he knows what harms him and what benefits him, in gratitude to his Lord, glorified and exalted is He, and that would be due to His kindness toward him. Is the reward of kindness anything but kindness? Is the reward of blessing anything but gratitude? Rather, he chose evil and committed harm, although We had prepared him for each of the two. Thus Our power became clear, and Our greatness became manifest in Our attributes, and his weakness was established, and his deficiency and incapacity appeared from him. So it became obligatory upon him, by Our might, to submit, and to let flow the protected tears (p-61) and to show need, humility and lowliness, so that We might cause him to enter the way of Paradise and save him from the path of the Fire. Whoever has crossed this steep path, which is for righteous deeds, has crossed the steep path of the Sirat, and its ease for him will be in proportion to his striving in these, and he will rest from those struggles, griefs and worries, and will arrive at a good life, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, We will surely cause him to live a good life﴾ [An-Nahl: 97], to the end of the verse. Its crossing is by moving from his lowly world to the complete high world, in which there is nothing but pleasure. That is the acknowledgment of the right of servitude ('ubudiyyah), and that is freedom, because the free person is one who has come out of the bondage (riqq) of desires into the service of the Master, so that he becomes [obedient] to His command in his secret and his open conduct, with no share of desire in him and no access of any portion of self to him. This happens through two things: one of them is attraction (jadhb) and the other is acquisition (kasb). The one who is attracted is carried, and the one who acquires, in the toil of striving, with the sword of lofty aspiration, is one who attains.

Once he had made clear that there is no escape from distress except through this "breaching" (iqtiḥām), he began to explain the ʿaqabah (the steep ascent), starting by magnifying its matter because of the greatness of its worth. He said, using the past tense, which is the Qur'an's customary usage whenever it employs it to explain what the questioner is asking about: ﴿And what will make you know what the steep ascent is?﴾ That is, O hearer of our words, who desires what is with Us: you do not know the true nature of its difficulty or the greatness of its reward. Then, when the heart is free to ask about what it does not know, and a person's strongest desire is to know what is unclear to him, souls yearn to know it. He said, pointing to the first (matter), which is chastity (ʿiffah), whose fruit is generosity (sakhāʾ), and the reform of the power of desire, expressing it with "freeing" (fakk), which is the least degree of manumission, because in it there is assistance, even if it is small, as occurs in the hadith of al-Barāʾ, may Allah be pleased with him: "He freed the soul (nasamah) and released the neck (raqabah)." Its manumission (ʿitq) is that one bears it alone, and its freeing (fakk) is that one is specified in its price. He explained the intended meaning of this ʿaqabah by what indicates an equivalent, not as the specification of its estimate comes later, for it is only used in repetition. He said:

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 90, verse 13:

﴿Freeing﴾, i.e., the human being frees ﴿a slave﴾, that is, from captivity, or from oppression, or from debt, or from sickness, out of gratitude to the One who bestowed good upon him, and to relieve distress, out of love for lofty and noble deeds, not for show and reputation, as this deluded, misguided doubter did, nor out of greed for a reward, nor out of fear of hardship.

Or the giving of food (ʾiṭʿām) — that is, the bestowing of food upon one who is deserving of it — ﴿in a day of severe hunger﴾, i.e., a day of general famine, in a place of famine and a time of famine, as the descriptor and the morphological form imply. For this reason, it compels one to be stingy with what is available out of fear of the same condition that the one being fed is in; yet he opposes the self and prefers others over it, relying upon Allah.

Translating the passage:

﴿Yatīman﴾ (an orphan), that is, [a person] who is a young child with no father, who is hoped for or feared [to be lost], ﴿dhā maqrabah﴾ (one near of kin); for whom feeding offers no hope of anything except winning the affection of his relatives, so as to increase their numbers, while [he] thereby combines in it both charity (ṣadaqah) and maintaining the ties of kinship (ṣilah), even if he is wealthy.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 90, verse 16:

﴿Or a needy person⁠﴾ (p-63): that is, a person with no means of sustenance. ﴿In misery⁠﴾: that is, in a state of need that has reduced him to lying in the dust, unable to rise above it to anything else. Thus the verse is of the type called (ihtibak): mentioning nearness first indicates its opposite second, and mentioning misery second indicates its opposite first. The secret of this is that for the orphan he mentioned the nearness that inclines the heart, while for the needy he mentioned the softened, gentle description, for he intends by feeding him nothing but to relieve his want. The distant orphan and the poor man also enter under it by way of a fortiori, even if he is a stranger.

Since these deeds are good in themselves, indicating goodness of disposition, loftiness of aspiration, nobility of stock, and disdain for baseness, they point to the intensity of their goodness, for none is granted success in them except a sincere person. This holds even if he was not relying on the Law (sharʿ), and on what it yields of smoothness of disposition, ease of submission, and the greatness of faith. By the expression with the particle of delay in His saying, pointing to the second obstacle ('aqaba), which is wisdom (ḥikma) that purifies the rational faculty (al-quwwa al-nuṭqiyya): ﴿Then he became﴾, i.e., after adorning himself with these pure, lofty, precious, and costly characters, in the state of his disbelief or at the beginnings of his Islam, to indicate the purity of his nature and the excellence of his stock, from those firmly established in faith, expressed by His saying: ﴿of those who believed﴾, i.e., when the Guide called him to it. The zeal of his nose and the arrogance of his soul did not compel him to refuse to be a follower after having been a leader, or to consider himself base after having been exalted. Rather, he directed his gaze and straightened his thought, so he was certain that he would raise his soul from the lowest pit to above the Pleiades (al-Suhā), ascending with it through the stages of lofty matters to what has no end. Surely in that are signs for those of understanding. Then he knew the uprightness of his nature, the nobility of his instinct, his lofty aspiration, the goodness of his intention, the beauty of his inner disposition, the abundance of his intellect, the grandeur of his nobility and excellence, and his worthiness to precede the notables in the Jahiliyyah and in Islam.

For this reason al-Ṣiddīq (the Truthful), may Allah be pleased with him, was the highest of people in rank after the prophets, upon them be the best prayers, greetings, and honour, because these were his deeds, may Allah be pleased with him, before Islam. Ibn al-Daghunna said, when he found him leaving the honoured Makkah intending emigration, after the disbelievers had harmed him: "Verily, one like you, O Abu Bakr, does not leave, nor is he driven out. You join ties of kinship, host the guest, bear the burdens, and help in the calamities of truth." This is as Khadija, may Allah be pleased with her, said to the Prophet (ﷺ) when he returned to her with his shoulders trembling from the manifestation of Jibril, peace be upon him, to him.

Then, when he flowed into the wide course of his channel and drank from the clear source of his spring, by success from Allah, the Exalted, he did not falter when he called him to the religion, nor was there in him any stumbling or hesitation. Then he ascended through the degrees of Islam to the highest aim, to the extent that on the day of al-Ḥudaybiyya, when ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, showed his dislike of the peace treaty, he [Abu Bakr] said to him what the Prophet (ﷺ) had said, word for word, without having been present or having had his words conveyed to him. He then proceeded, taking the prize of the race, with no hope of approaching him, let alone catching up with him or equalling him.

Because of his perfection, greatness, and majesty, he never drank wine at all. Whenever he was blamed for this in the Jahiliyyah, he said [to ʿUshāʾ]: "By Allah, if I found anything that would increase my intellect, I would buy it with all my wealth. How then would I buy with my wealth that which removes my intellect?"

These deeds are not valid, even though they are praiseworthy in every case, except with faith. As for what comes after faith, it is clear. As for what comes before it, it is by [Allah's] inclining toward them, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said:

"I have embraced Islam upon whatever good preceded from you."

Since faith elevates a person above degradation to great rank, bearing him toward noble deeds and honourable actions, and since it leads to all the great laws of the religion, and since these laws necessitate the greater struggle (al-jihād al-akbar) because they oppose the natural disposition, and this cannot be accomplished except by courage (al-shajāʿa), which is the third faculty (al-quwwa al-thālitha), and which, when it is calmed, brings relief, and which only comes with great patience, and since patience, because of its bitterness, does not endure except through mutual assistance, He, the Exalted, said: ﴿and they enjoined one another﴾, i.e., they were patient and counselled one another ﴿to patience﴾ in braving the obstacles of deeds, which only the champions of men can traverse, from enjoining the good to what is recorded (in the Law), even if it involves perils of death, for courage, as it is said, is an hour of patience.

Since a person must inevitably face from others some disputes that necessitate harshness toward them, mercy becomes one of the fruits of the patience that yields justice (ʿadāla), which is the balance between the two blameworthy extremes of excess and deficiency in wickedness and foolishness. This is the fourth obstacle. He said, emphasising by repeating the verb to indicate the scarcity of those who practise it: ﴿and they enjoined one another to compassion﴾, i.e., the great compassion according to its time and place, by habituating themselves to everything that leads to great compassion, which necessitates for them love for the sake of Allah and hatred for His sake. For before faith they were sincere, free of ostentation and self-admiration, prepared for purification, so faith purified them, and they became in the utmost degree of illumination and gnosis.

Since that is among the noble qualities and things that necessitate kindness and harmony, its outcome is inevitably: ﴿Those﴾, that is, the great and exalted ones of lofty station. He did not use the separating pronoun (ḍamīr al-faṣl) as it is used for their opposites, in order to make the act sincerely for Him, glorified and exalted be He, without looking at their inner dispositions that indicate their innate natures, because it is He who created those natures. He dispensed with that by the demonstrative that indicates the elevation of their rank and the remoteness of their aims (p. 67) ﴿the companions of the right hand﴾, that is, the side in which there is blessing, goodness and salvation from every ruin, in its two divisions: the foremost, those brought near, and the companions of the right, the righteous. Its explanation has passed in the commentary on Surat al-Waqi'ah. This is an allusion to that one who squandered his wealth in ostentation and in opposing and contending.

Commentary of al-Biqa'i (Nazm al-Durar) on surah 90, verse 19:

When the context guided toward the parallel of ﴿So he did not attempt the steep path﴾ [al-Balad: 11], it indicated that the implied meaning is: "And I do not shrink from the destructive acts, which are the actions that bring about reproach, even though they are wearisome. Rather, he severed ties with one who deserves connection and maintained ties with one who deserves severance. Then he was among those who disbelieved, who counseled one another to harshness, who earned evil deeds, who followed desires, and who dealt with cruelty." Then He joined to it His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved﴾, that is, they concealed what the mirrors of their insight would have shown them of knowledge. Since disbelief in the signs is among the worst kinds of disbelief, because it is disbelief in what God made a sign pointing to the unseen of His covenant, and these signs comprise everything the senses perceive of speech and actions that indicate the One of Majesty, because they point to the attributes that indicate the One described by them, who became manifest through His acts and was hidden through the greatness of His majesty, He said: ﴿with Our signs﴾, [meaning] what they possess of greatness through their being attributed to Us and of the manifestness that cannot be concealed. ﴿They﴾, that is, specifically, because of the evil of their inner selves and the corruption of their natures, ﴿are the companions of the left hand﴾, that is, the trait that earns misfortune, deprivation and ruin. These are ill-omened for themselves, and their disbelief indicates the corruption of their natures. Thus it (p-68) indicates that whoever's disbelief is lighter was not innately so, and so he is likely to be guided and become among the companions of the right hand.

Since the meaning of this is that they are in the direction in which there is ill omen and destruction, and remoteness from every blessing, it produced His saying: ﴿Upon them﴾, that is, specifically and not others, ﴿is a fire vaulted over﴾, that is, its door is sealed shut, along with its encompassing them from all sides, by what the particle of elevation (ʿalāʾ) conveys, and along with narrowness and harshness. By my life, this is the utmost of narrowness, hardship, toil and misery, so refuge from it is with Allah, the One, the Unique, the Eternal Refuge. It is known that its beginning is this last, so the dripping within it is among the things by which hands are bound and fingers are knotted. And Allah, exalted is He, is the one hoped for guidance to the best of inner states, and He is the Guide to what is right, and to Him is the return and the final resort.
